blocks.text: Not every MCP server supports every feature, one might offer tools but no prompts, another might support resource subscriptions and another might not. Capabilities are how a client and server tell each other, right at the start of a session, exactly what they each actually support, so neither side ever has to guess.
1. What a Capability Actually Is

blocks.alt: A server has a capability describing what it supports

blocks.text: A capability is a named feature a client or server declares support for, tools, resources, prompts, and more specific sub-features like resource subscriptions, each capability is simply a flag or small object saying "yes, I support this."

blocks.title: A useful analogy
blocks.content: Capabilities work a lot like a restaurant menu, before ordering, you check what is actually on it, rather than assuming the kitchen can make anything you might ask for.

blocks.text: A capability being absent is just as meaningful as one being present, both are useful, explicit information about what a connection can and cannot do.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If you can name three things a specific server does not support just by reading its declared capabilities, you understand the concept.

blocks.text: Capabilities are declared as part of a broader picture, alongside the tool, resource, and prompt lists themselves, together giving a client a complete, honest picture of a server before any real work begins.
2. Capabilities Are Exchanged During Initialize

blocks.alt: Client capabilities exchange with server capabilities at initialize

blocks.text: The client sends its own supported capabilities as part of the initialize request, the server responds with its own capabilities in the initialize response, by the time this handshake completes, both sides know exactly what the other supports.
This exchange happens exactly once per session, right at the start, which is why the initialize handshake is considered such a foundational, non-skippable step.

code.content:
# the server response completing the handshake
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": {"protocolVersion": "2025-06-18", "capabilities": {"tools": {}, "prompts": {}}}}

blocks.text: If either side fails to send valid capabilities during this handshake, most implementations treat it as a serious protocol error, since everything downstream depends on this information being accurate.
3. Server Capabilities: Tools, Resources, and Prompts

blocks.alt: A server declares tools, resources, and prompts

blocks.text: A server’s capabilities object typically declares which of the three main features, tools, resources, prompts, it supports at all, a server offering only tools would simply omit resources and prompts from its declared capabilities entirely.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Declared capability","Meaning"],"rows":[["tools","This server exposes callable tools"],["resources","This server exposes readable resources"],["prompts","This server exposes instruction templates"]]}

blocks.text: A minimal server exposing only a couple of simple tools would declare just tools, leaving resources and prompts out entirely, and that is a perfectly complete, valid server.

A more feature-rich server, offering all three plus subscriptions, would simply have a larger, more detailed capabilities object, the shape scales naturally with how much the server actually supports.
4. Client Capabilities Matter Too

Capabilities are not one-directional, a client also declares what it supports, for instance whether it can handle certain kinds of notifications or sampling requests, a server can use this information to adjust its own behavior accordingly.

A client declaring sampling support, for instance, tells the server it is able to receive a request asking the model to generate something, without that declaration, a server should not attempt to send one.

blocks.title: Why this matters for servers
blocks.content: A server that ignores declared client capabilities and sends something the client cannot handle risks the message being silently dropped or, worse, misinterpreted.

blocks.text: 5. Sub-Capabilities Add Finer Detail

Some capabilities include nested detail beyond a simple yes or no, resources might declare subscribe support specifically, meaning the server can notify a client when a resource changes, without that sub-flag, a client should not attempt to subscribe.

Checking only for the presence of the parent capability is not always enough, a client wanting to subscribe to resource changes specifically needs to check for the subscribe sub-flag, not just the presence of resources overall.

code.content:
# checking a specific sub-capability, not just the parent one
resources_cap = server_capabilities.get("resources", {})
can_subscribe = resources_cap.get("subscribe", False)

blocks.text: This layered structure lets a server be very precise about exactly what it offers, rather than only being able to say yes or no at a coarse, whole-feature level.
6. Why Not Just Try and See What Fails

blocks.alt: Trying and seeing what fails is compared against declaring capabilities upfront

blocks.text: Without explicit capability declaration, a client would have to discover what a server supports by trial and error, sending a request and seeing if it fails, this is slow, unreliable, and gives poor error messages, declaring capabilities upfront avoids all of that guesswork.

Trial-and-error discovery also produces worse error messages, a request rejected because "this method does not exist" is far less helpful than a client that already knew, from capabilities, not to try in the first place.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Speed","Error clarity"],"rows":[["Trial and error","Slower, wastes a round trip","Vague, generic failure"],["Capability check first","Immediate","Clear, informed decision"]]}

blocks.text: This upfront clarity is especially valuable for AI agents specifically, a model reasoning about what actions are available benefits enormously from knowing the full, accurate feature set before attempting anything.
The small upfront cost of checking capabilities pays for itself many times over across the lifetime of a long-running application handling many requests.
7. Capabilities Enable Graceful Degradation

blocks.alt: A missing capability leads to graceful degradation

blocks.text: If a server does not support prompts, a well-behaved client simply skips offering prompt-related features to the user, rather than crashing or showing a confusing error, capabilities are what make this kind of graceful, adaptive behavior possible.

blocks.title: A concrete UX benefit
blocks.content: A chat application connected to a tools-only server can simply hide its "browse prompts" button entirely, rather than showing it and having it fail when clicked.

blocks.text: This same principle scales to much larger systems too, an enterprise application connected to dozens of MCP servers, each with a slightly different feature set, relies entirely on capability checks to avoid a confusing, inconsistent user experience.

code.content:
# a UI that adapts based on declared capabilities
features_to_show = [f for f in ["tools", "resources", "prompts"] if f in server_caps]
render_menu(features_to_show)

blocks.text: 8. Capabilities and Protocol Versioning Work Together

A new version of the protocol might introduce an entirely new capability, older clients and servers simply will not declare it, and newer ones can check for its presence before trying to use it, this is exactly how MCP evolves without breaking existing implementations.

This is exactly the same forward-compatibility principle discussed in the Protocol Versioning lesson in the Communication Protocol module, capabilities and versioning work hand in hand to let the ecosystem evolve safely.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Scenario","What capabilities reveal"],"rows":[["Old client, new server","Server may support features the client does not know to use"],["New client, old server","Client should not assume newer features exist"]]}

blocks.text: This combination is exactly what allows the MCP ecosystem to keep growing, new capabilities can be introduced freely without breaking any implementation that predates them.
9. A Server Checking Client Capabilities

A server can use the client’s declared capabilities to decide what it is safe to do, for example, only sending a certain kind of notification if the client explicitly declared it can handle that notification type.
This kind of adaptive behavior means the exact same server can serve both a very capable, modern client and a simpler, older one, each getting an experience tailored to what they can actually handle.

blocks.title: A safety benefit
blocks.content: This also protects against sending a client something it explicitly said it cannot handle, avoiding a confusing, unusable message reaching an application that was never built to process it.

blocks.text: This same defensive pattern, check before sending, mirrors the check-before-calling pattern a client uses for server capabilities, the negotiation genuinely runs both directions.
10. Capabilities Should Be Checked, Not Assumed

blocks.alt: A capability gets checked before use

blocks.text: A well-written client always checks the server’s declared capabilities before attempting to use a feature, rather than assuming every server supports everything, this single habit avoids a large class of avoidable runtime errors.
This defensive habit costs almost nothing to implement and prevents an entire category of confusing, hard-to-diagnose runtime failures.
11. Capabilities Are Immutable for the Session

blocks.alt: A capability stays fixed for the entire session

blocks.text: Once negotiated during initialization, capabilities generally stay fixed for the lifetime of that session, if a server’s underlying features change, that typically requires a fresh session with a new initialize handshake, rather than capabilities silently changing mid-conversation.

blocks.title: A practical implication
blocks.content: If a server is updated with a new feature while a client is mid-session, that client will not see the new capability until it reconnects and re-runs the initialize handshake.

blocks.text: This reconnect-to-refresh pattern is a small but important detail worth remembering when building any long-lived host application against evolving servers.
12. Capabilities Make Servers Self-Documenting

A capabilities object is, in a small but real way, a piece of live documentation, any client connecting can immediately see what a server supports without needing to consult a separate, potentially outdated document describing it.

code.content:
# a client can print a server's full feature set directly from its capabilities
print(json.dumps(server_capabilities, indent=2))

blocks.text: This is one more small way MCP reduces the burden of writing and maintaining separate documentation, the protocol itself carries a meaningful amount of that information automatically.
13. A Worked Example
Trace an initialize exchange where the client checks the server’s response before deciding whether to offer prompt-related UI to the user.
This same pattern, check first, then decide what UI or behavior to offer, generalizes to every other capability a client might care about, not just prompts specifically.
14. Common Mistakes When Working With Capabilities

items: Assuming every server supports every feature, and calling a method the server never declared support for.
Forgetting that capabilities flow both ways, only checking what the server supports and never declaring the client’s own capabilities.
Ignoring sub-capabilities, like resource subscriptions, and attempting to use a finer-grained feature the server did not specifically declare.
Hardcoding assumptions about capabilities instead of reading them dynamically from the actual initialize response.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is treating a missing capability as an error rather than a normal, valid configuration, a server simply not supporting prompts is not broken, it may just be intentionally scoped to a smaller feature set.
A sixth common mistake is caching a server capabilities from a previous session and reusing them without re-checking, a fresh session always deserves a fresh initialize handshake.
15. Practice: Write a Capability Check
Write a small function that takes a server’s declared capabilities and returns a list of which of the three main features, tools, resources, prompts, it actually supports.
Extend your function further to also check for the resources subscribe sub-capability specifically, returning a separate, more detailed answer for that finer-grained feature.
As a final extension, add a check specifically for the resources subscribe sub-capability, returning it as a separate detail rather than folding it into the top-level resources flag.
Key Takeaway

Capabilities are how a client and server tell each other, right at the start of a session, exactly what they each support, tools, resources, prompts, and finer sub-features like subscriptions, letting both sides adapt gracefully instead of guessing or failing unpredictably.

This lesson closes the tour of the core building blocks, tools, resources, prompts, context, messages, requests, responses, and capabilities. The final lesson in this module, Session Lifecycle, ties all of these together into the complete arc of one MCP connection, from start to finish.

The immutable-for-the-session property from the newly added section is worth remembering, if a server’s capabilities genuinely need to change, that almost always means starting an entirely new session rather than expecting an existing one to adapt mid-conversation.

As a last reminder, capabilities are declared once per session and should be treated as the definitive source of truth for what is safe to attempt, over any assumption based on a server name, version number, or prior experience with a similar server.
